messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Model
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Elaine is a 66-year-old widow who had worked for decades as a commercial model, the kind of woman who was used to being poised under bright lights and taking direction with exactness. The event that brought her to treatment happened during a local photo shoot for a boutique department store. The set had been built in a converted warehouse, with garment racks, rolling mirrors, cords taped imperfectly along the floor, and assistants moving quickly around her. During a reset between shots, Elaine shifted a wheeled clothing rack to make room for the photographer’s angle. She has replayed the moment countless times: she remembers noticing another woman, a younger stylist’s assistant, near the edge of the platform, remembers thinking she should say something, should steady the rack, should do more. Instead the rack lurched, struck the assistant, and sent her falling badly enough to sustain serious injuries. Even now, what stays with Elaine is not only the sight of the woman on the floor but the unbearable conviction that she had one clear chance to prevent it and failed.

In the days afterward, Elaine learned that the assistant would survive, but the injury was severe, and that fact did not relieve her. What took hold in her was less shock than a hardening judgment about herself. She had come to believe that a more competent person, a better person, would never have been in that position to begin with. She compared herself relentlessly to an imagined other woman who would have seen the danger sooner, moved faster, spoken up more clearly, done something decisive before the rack rolled. Because she had not, she felt marked by what happened. She described a permanent humiliation, as if the accident had exposed something shameful and deficient in her character that could not be covered over, and she said more than once that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop it.

Over the following months, her body did not settle. Even sitting alone in her apartment, where she knew she was safe, she found she could not relax into the chair or unclench her shoulders. She stayed taut and watchful, her muscles braced as if something else might go wrong at any second. At work this became particularly obvious. On set, where assistants crossed behind her and equipment was wheeled in and out, her attention splintered. She would lose the thread of a photographer’s instructions halfway through, ask for directions to be repeated, and scan the edges of the room instead of focusing on the camera. The familiar environment of studios and backstage corridors, once ordinary to her, now kept her body on alert.

That persistent state of tension fed directly into how she thought about the accident. When she noticed herself jumpy, unable to concentrate, and physically keyed up even in situations she recognized as safe, Elaine took this not as a symptom but as evidence against herself. In her mind, if she were not fundamentally at fault, if she were not the sort of person who lets terrible things happen, she would have been able to calm down by now. Her inability to relax became proof that the humiliation was deserved. The more on edge she felt, the more certain she became that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation and that her failure in that split second said something permanent about her.

As that pattern tightened, her work life narrowed. She still accepted some bookings, but only with difficulty, and she moved through them with a strained vigilance that made even routine shoots exhausting. When a rack was rolled across a concrete floor or a stylist hurried past carrying armfuls of clothing, her whole body stiffened. She would miss cues, drift during wardrobe changes, and feel ashamed when younger crew members had to repeat simple instructions. Those moments of lost concentration quickly became fresh material for self-reproach. To Elaine, the fact that she could not keep herself composed in the very setting where the injury occurred seemed to confirm that she was the kind of person who creates danger and fails others when it matters.

By the time she sought help, nearly a year had passed. She came in after leaving a shoot early because she could not stop trembling when equipment was being moved around her, and afterward she sat in her car unable to steady herself. She said she was tired of living as if her body had never received the message that the accident was over. What frightened her most was the idea that this constant tension meant she was beyond forgiveness, condemned to remain the woman who did not do enough. What she hoped, though she said it cautiously, was that treatment might help her understand why she still feels under threat all the time and whether it is possible to live without that unending sense of disgrace.
